docs.text: !!! abstract "Lab 01 Metadata & Hardware Configuration" * Course: Software Defined Radio (SDR) Laboratory [1] * Team ID: Team-01 [1] * Date: November 3, 2026 * Team Members: SeyedParham Moghaddasi & Amirali Rajai * Hardware: ADALM-Pluto (AD9363 Transceiver, Zynq-7010 FPGA+ARM) * Network IP: 192.168.1.10 [8, 9] * Reference TCXO Accuracy: $\pm 25\text{ ppm}$ [10]

docs.title: :material-tune: Section 1: Setup & Spectrum Monitoring
1.1 Flowgraph Architecture
docs.text:
In the lab01_monitor.grc flowgraph, the Filter Configuration parameter of the PlutoSDR Source block is set to Off [2, 7].

!!! note "Hardware Analog Bandwidth Configuration" Setting Filter Configuration = Off prevents GNU Radio from overriding the internal hardware analog bandwidth filters [2]. In Off mode, the AD9363 transceiver maintains its maximum $20\text{ MHz}$ default analog RF bandwidth, avoiding unexpected spectral truncation at the edges [2, 11].

docs.title: 1.2 Question 1: Reliable Span and Sweep Step
docs.text:
• Edge Roll-off vs. Spectrum Center: Analog low-pass filters (LPF) and digital decimation filters inside the AD9363 receiver attenuate amplitude levels at the spectrum edges near $\pm f_s / 2$ [12, 13]. Additionally, DC offset and Local Oscillator (LO) leakage introduce an artificial spike at the baseband center ($f_{bb} = 0$) [12, 13].
  • Reliable Span Ratio: The reliable frequency span is defined as the central 80% of $f_s$, covering $[-0.4 f_s, +0.4 f_s]$ [13].
  • Sweep Step Relation: To perform wideband spectrum scanning without edge distortion, the frequency step between consecutive center frequencies is set to:

$$ \Delta\text{step} = 0.8 f_s $$

This choice provides a 20% spectral overlap between steps, allowing attenuated outer edges to be cropped while seamlessly stitching reliable central bands together [13, 14].

docs.title: 1.3 Question 2: Frequency Error & Reference Accuracy for GSM900
docs.text:
• Theoretical Formulation: Downlink GSM900 carrier frequencies follow the standard grid $f_{\text{standard}} = 935 + 0.2n\text{ MHz}$ [13, 15]. The absolute frequency error $\Delta f$ and reference clock error $\varepsilon$ in ppm are expressed as [10, 13]:

$$ \Delta f = f_{\text{observed}} - f_{\text{standard}} $$

$$ \text{Error (ppm)} = \frac{\Delta f}{f_c} \times 10^6 $$

  • Nominal Boundary: For the ADALM-Pluto's $\pm 25\text{ ppm}$ reference TCXO [10], at $f_c = 945\text{ MHz}$ [16], the maximum expected offset is:

$$ \Delta f_{\text{max}} = 945 \times 10^6 \times (\pm 25 \times 10^{-6}) = \pm 23.625\text{ kHz} $$

!!! warning "Data Verification Requirement" The screenshot 2.6.jpg lacks explicit numerical markers on the GSM carrier peaks. To strictly comply with lab regulations prohibiting data fabrication [5, 17], exact observed carrier frequencies must be extracted offline from Team-07's raw .cf32 I/Q recording to compute the device-specific ppm error [13, 18].

docs.title: :material-sync: Section 2: Loopback Test with Known Signal
2.1 Flowgraph Setup
docs.text: The lab01_loopback.grc flowgraph incorporates a complex Signal Source connected to a PlutoSDR Sink transmitting a single tone at $f_{tx} = +250\text{ kHz}$ with a transmitter attenuation of $\text{tx_att} = 60\text{ dB}$ and receiver gain $\text{rf_gain} \le 10\text{ dB}$ [19-21].

docs.title: 2.2 Question 3: Quadrature I/Q Sampling & Phase Separation
docs.text:
• Separation Mechanism: The AD9363 receiver uses Direct Conversion (Zero-IF) with Quadrature I/Q sampling [3, 12]. The received complex signal $x(t) = I(t) + jQ(t) = e^{j 2\pi f_{tx} t}$ maintains a $90^\circ$ phase difference between $I$ and $Q$ channels [12]. This phase relationship preserves signal rotation directionality in the complex plane, cleanly distinguishing $+250\text{ kHz}$ from $-250\text{ kHz}$ in the FFT spectrum [3, 12].
  • If Only the $I$-Branch Were Sampled: The resulting signal would be purely real: $x(t) = I(t) = \cos(2\pi f_{tx} t)$ [3]. By Euler's identity:

$$ \cos(2\pi f_{tx} t) = \frac{1}{2} e^{j 2\pi f_{tx} t} + \frac{1}{2} e^{-j 2\pi f_{tx} t} $$

Real-valued signals possess a symmetric spectrum around zero frequency [3]. Consequently, both $+250\text{ kHz}$ and $-250\text{ kHz}$ inputs would produce identical twin peaks at $\pm 250\text{ kHz}$, making sign identification impossible [3].

docs.title: 2.3 Question 4: Peak Classification via LO Shift Slope
docs.text:
During the LO shift test ($f_c = 434.00\text{ MHz}$, $f_{tx} = +250\text{ kHz}$), spectral peaks are classified using their shift slope $s = \frac{\Delta\text{label}}{\Delta\text{LO}}$ [3, 22]:

  1. Real Transmitted Signal Peak ($434.250\text{ MHz}$):
  2. The physical RF frequency remains unchanged at $f_{\text{RF}} = f_c + f_{tx} = 434.250\text{ MHz}$ [19, 22].
  3. Slope: $s = 0 \rightarrow$ Real Input Signal [3].
  4. LO Leakage / DC Offset Peak ($434.000\text{ MHz}$):
  5. Located at baseband DC ($f_{bb} = 0$), labeled at $f_{\text{label}} = f_{\text{LO}}$ [12, 23]. As LO shifts by $\Delta\text{LO}$, the label moves by the exact same amount [23].
  6. Slope: $s = +1 \rightarrow$ Receiver Artifact (DC Offset / LO Leakage) [3].
  7. Image Peak ($433.750\text{ MHz}$):
  8. Caused by I/Q gain and phase imbalance at the image frequency $-f_{tx}$ [12, 24].
  9. Slope: $s = -1 \rightarrow$ Receiver Artifact (Image Peak) [3].

!!! failure "Anomalous Screenshot Observation in 100k.png" In image 100k.png, the main peak label displays $433.996\text{ MHz}$ instead of $434.250\text{ MHz}$ ($s=0$). This anomaly occurred due to a transient GUI parameter update during screenshot capture and is documented in the Troubleshooting section [6].

docs.title: 2.4 Question 5: Error Cancellation in Loopback Measurement
docs.text:
!!! tip "Clock Synchronization Mechanics" In over-the-air reception, transmitter and receiver operate on independent clock sources, exposing reference frequency offset [3, 10]. In loopback mode, both TX and RX reside on the same AD9363 chip inside ADALM-Pluto, sharing a single TCXO reference oscillator [3, 9].

Assuming a fractional reference oscillator error $\delta$:

$$ f_{\text{TX, real}} = (f_c + f_{tx})(1 + \delta) $$

$$ f_{\text{RX, LO}} = f_c (1 + \delta) $$

$$ f_{bb, \text{meas}} = f_{\text{TX, real}} - f_{\text{RX, LO}} = f_{tx}(1 + \delta) $$

The software frequency label applies the same clock scale:

$$ f_{\text{label}} = f_{\text{RX, LO}} + f_{bb, \text{meas}} = (f_c + f_{tx})(1 + \delta) $$

Because the software frequency axis scale and sampling clock share the identical reference, the error factor $(1 + \delta)$ cancels out relative to the nominal software grid, yielding an exact reading of $434.250\text{ MHz}$ [3, 24].

docs.title: :material-radar: Section 3: Band Scanning & Signal Identification
3.1 Wideband Sweeping Strategy & Flowgraph Operation
docs.text:
Because the instantaneous analog bandwidth and maximum continuous decimation rate of the receiver ($f_s = 20\text{ MS/s}$) are smaller than standard cellular bands, wideband spectrum scanning was performed step-by-step using the lab01_monitor.grc flowgraph. Following Equation (2), the sweep step was set to:

$$ \Delta\text{step} = 0.8 f_s = 16\text{ MHz} $$

This choice ensures a $20\%$ spectral overlap between adjacent frequency steps, mitigating edge roll-off introduced by the analog filters while maintaining the central $80\%$ span as the reliable measurement window.

docs.title: 3.2 Band B Sweep: Key Fob Remote Control (433 MHz ISM Band)
docs.text:
• Configuration: $f_c = 434.500\text{ MHz}$, $f_s = 2.6\text{ MS/s}$, rf_gain = $30\text{ dB}$, with Max Hold enabled to capture transient events.
  • Observation: When the vehicle remote control key fob was pressed, distinct pulse bursts appeared around $f_c \approx 433.933\text{ MHz}$. These short bursts are characteristic of ASK/OOK or FSK modulation utilized by Short Range Devices (SRDs).
  • Raw Recording: Captured as Team_01_lab01_435000000_2600000_30.0_20261108T142900.cf32 with a duration of $3.85\text{ s}$ ($10^7\text{ samples}$).

Figure 2: Waterfall display of Band B during key-fob transmission at ~433.93 MHz.

docs.title: 3.3 Band C Sweep: GSM-900 Downlink (935–960 MHz)
docs.text:
The full $25\text{ MHz}$ downlink spectrum of the GSM-900 base station band was swept in two consecutive steps:

  1. Step 1 ($f_{c,1} = 943\text{ MHz}$): Covers the lower downlink band ($933\text{–}953\text{ MHz}$).
  2. Step 2 ($f_{c,2} = 959\text{ MHz}$): Covers the upper downlink band ($949\text{–}969\text{ MHz}$).

Figure 3: First step of GSM-900 downlink sweep centered at 943 MHz ($f_s = 20\text{ MS/s}$, Max Hold).

Figure 4: Second step of GSM-900 downlink sweep centered at 959 MHz ($f_s = 20\text{ MS/s}$, Max Hold).

docs.title: Quantitative Analysis of Cellular GSM-900 Parameters:
docs.text:
• Channel Bandwidth & Spacing: Standard GSM-900 downlink channels occupy a nominal bandwidth of $200\text{ kHz}$ and are arranged on a $200\text{ kHz}$ carrier frequency grid:

$$ f_n = 935.0 + 0.2 \times n\text{ MHz} $$

  • Beacon (BCCH) vs. Traffic (TCH) Carriers:
  • Broadcast Control Channel (BCCH): Transmits continuously at constant power across all timeslots to provide cell identification and synchronization. On the waterfall display, BCCH carriers appear as prominent, uninterrupted vertical lines of uniform intensity.

  • Traffic Channels (TCH): Exhibit bursty, fragmented duty cycles in the time domain, activating intermittently according to user voice call and SMS demand.

  • Identification of Measured Carriers:

  • Carrier #85: Observed at $f = 952.095\text{ MHz}$:

$$ n = \frac{952.095 - 935.0}{0.2} = 85.475 \approx 85 \quad (f_{\text{standard}} = 952.000\text{ MHz}) $$

High peak power ($-45.8\text{ dBFS}$) and continuous temporal presence identify this as a local base-station BCCH carrier.

  • Carrier #89: Observed at $f = 952.7965\text{ MHz}$:

$$ n = \frac{952.7965 - 935.0}{0.2} = 88.98 \approx 89 \quad (f_{\text{standard}} = 952.800\text{ MHz}) $$

Occupying a $20\text{-dB}$ bandwidth of $B_x = 235\text{ kHz}$ (closely aligning with the nominal $200\text{ kHz}$ channel width) with constant power ($-45.2\text{ dBFS}$), this represents an adjacent cell BCCH beacon.

  • Carrier #124: Observed at $f = 959.804\text{ MHz}$:

$$ n = \frac{959.804 - 935.0}{0.2} = 124.02 \approx 124 \quad (f_{\text{standard}} = 959.800\text{ MHz}) $$

Exhibits lower average power ($-64.5\text{ dBFS}$) and bursty time-slot activity, characteristic of a GSM traffic channel.

docs.title: 3.4 Band C-2 Sweep: GSM-900 Uplink (890–915 MHz)
docs.text:
• Safety Protocol Compliance: As mandated by laboratory safety rules, the mobile handset was maintained at a physical distance exceeding $5\text{ m}$ from the SDR receive antenna, and the receiver gain was strictly set to rf_gain = 0 dB prior to call initiation. This prevents input overdrive damage from cellular terminal bursts (which can reach up to $+33\text{ dBm}$) relative to the AD9363 input damage threshold ($+2.5\text{ dBm}$).
  • Observation: The uplink channel operates in Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA). Uplink transmissions were observed at $f = 908.1685\text{ MHz}$, presenting short pulse bursts during outgoing voice traffic.
  • Duplex Frequency Pair: In GSM-900 FDD, the duplex spacing is exactly $45\text{ MHz}$:

$$ f_{\text{DL}} = f_{\text{UL}} + 45\text{ MHz} = 908.1685 + 45.0000 = 953.1685\text{ MHz} $$

This pairs directly with downlink ARFCN channel $n = 91$ ($f_{\text{nom}} = 953.2\text{ MHz}$). * Raw Recording: Captured as Team_01_lab01_907990000_2600000_30.0_20261108T145620.cf32.

$$ f_{c,\text{sig}} = \frac{f_L + f_U}{2}, \quad B_x = f_U - f_L $$

Note on $x\text{-dB}$ thresholds: Signals with sufficient SNR above the noise floor ($> 26\text{ dB}$) were evaluated at $x = 20\text{ dB}$. Signals operating near the ambient noise floor (such as the weak remote control carrier and distant uplink burst) were evaluated at $x = 6\text{ dB}$ or $x = 3\text{ dB}$ strictly as instructed by the laboratory manual.

docs.title: 3.6 Answers to Assigned Laboratory Questions
Question 6: Continuous vs. Transient Signals and the Critical Role of Max-Hold
docs.text:
• Temporal Distribution across Bands:
  • Band C (GSM-900 Downlink): Dominated by continuous transmissions. Cellular base stations continuously broadcast synchronization beacons (BCCH) on dedicated carriers to enable mobile terminal synchronization.
  • Band B (433 MHz Remote) and Band C-2 (GSM Uplink): Characterized entirely by transient / bursty transmissions. Remote key fobs emit only when mechanically triggered (burst durations $\approx 10\text{–}50\text{ ms}$), and mobile uplink channels transmit in designated TDMA slots only when a call or SMS handshake is active.
  • Function of Max-Hold:
  • In instantaneous spectrum mode or when video averaging is active, brief transient pulses are averaged out over time, causing intermittent bursts to disappear beneath the displayed noise floor.
  • The Max-Hold function stores and retains the absolute maximum power envelope across all FFT bins over time. It effectively "freezes" the spectral envelope of intermittent bursts, enabling accurate extraction of peak power, channel occupancy, and $x\text{-dB}$ bandwidth ($f_L, f_U$).

docs.title: Question 7: Remote Control Bursts and Probability of Intercept (POI)
docs.text:
• Experimental Observation: In live spectrum monitoring, approximately 1 out of every 3 button presses was clearly noticeable on the instantaneous spectrum trace.
  • Comparison with Pre-Lab POI Modeling:
  • A typical key-fob RF burst has a short duration ($T_{\text{burst}} \approx 10\text{–}30\text{ ms}$).
  • The GNU Radio GUI display updates periodically at discrete intervals ($\approx 100\text{ ms}$ display period), and Ethernet transport drops processing frames when LAN buffer saturation occurs. Consequently, the single-frame Probability of Intercept is relatively low ($\text{POI} < 30\%$).
  • Conversely, enabling Max-Hold over a continuous acquisition window or streaming contiguous I/Q samples directly to a binary .cf32 file yields a $\text{POI} \approx 100\%$, guaranteeing capture of short bursts.

docs.title: Question 8 (Extension): Systematic Discrimination between UMTS and 5 MHz LTE without Demodulation
docs.text:
Without demodulating the baseband I/Q data, a 5 MHz LTE carrier and a UMTS (WCDMA) carrier can be systematically differentiated through their unique spectral and temporal signatures:

  1. Spectral Roll-Off and Edge Steepness:
  2. UMTS (WCDMA): Modulated using single-carrier Direct-Sequence CDMA with a Root-Raised-Cosine (RRC) pulse-shaping filter ($\alpha = 0.22$, chip rate $3.84\text{ Mcps}$). The spectrum exhibits visibly rounded, sloping shoulders occupying $\approx 4.68\text{ MHz}$ between transmission nulls.
  3. LTE (5 MHz): Modulated using Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) with 300 active subcarriers ($15\text{ kHz}$ spacing, total occupied bandwidth $4.5\text{ MHz}$). Due to the superposition of closely spaced sinc-shaped subcarriers and outer guard bands, LTE produces a remarkably flat "table-top" passband with near-vertical, brick-wall roll-off edges.
  4. Temporal Uniformity in the Waterfall:
  5. An LTE transmission continuously broadcasts Cell-specific Reference Signals (CRS) across the entire bandwidth, yielding an exceptionally smooth and constant power spectral density over time.
  6. In contrast, UMTS power spectral density fluctuates significantly across time and frequency as the number of active CDMA code-tree channels changes dynamically with traffic.
  7. Carrier Raster Alignment:
  8. UMTS channel rasters are centered on a $200\text{ kHz}$ grid (or $100\text{ kHz}$ raster in specialized bands).
  9. LTE center frequencies follow standardized 3GPP EARFCN channel center points.

docs.title: 1. Summary of Theoretical Concepts
docs.text: RF receiver architectures are bounded at lower signal levels by thermal and internal component noise, and at upper levels by non-linear gain saturation and intermodulation distortion.

docs.title: Noise Figure (NF) and Noise Temperature (Te)
docs.text:
The Noise Factor ($F$) and Noise Figure ($NF$) measure the degradation of the Signal-to-Noise Ratio ($SNR$) as a signal propagates through a receiver processing chain:

$$F = \frac{SNR_{\text{in}}}{SNR_{\text{out}}} = 1 + \frac{T_e}{T_0}, \quad NF = 10 \log_{10}(F)$$

The input-referred noise floor ($N_{\text{floor}}$) over bandwidth $B$ is expressed as:

$$N_{\text{floor}} = -174\text{ dBm/Hz} + NF + 10 \log_{10}(B)$$

docs.title: Y-Factor Noise Measurement Method
docs.text:
The Y-Factor method utilizes a calibrated noise source operating in two states: OFF ($T_c \approx T_0$) and ON ($T_h \gg T_0$), defined by Excess Noise Ratio ($ENR$):

$$ENR = \frac{T_h - T_0}{T_0}, \quad Y = \frac{T_h + T_e}{T_0 + T_e} \implies F = \frac{ENR - Y \left(\frac{T_c}{T_0} - 1\right)}{Y - 1}$$

docs.title: Third-Order Intercept Point (IIP3) and Gain Compression (P1dB)
docs.text: Under two-tone excitation at $f_1$ and $f_2$, 3rd-order non-linearities generate intermodulation products (IM3) at $2f_1 - f_2$ and $2f_2 - f_1$.

docs.title: 2. Theoretical Analysis Highlights
docs.text:
• Frontend Filter Relocation (Question 1c): Relocating the $3\text{ dB}$ filter to the frontend alters Friis chain hierarchy (Stage 1 = Filter, Stage 2 = LNA, Stage 3 = Mixer/ADC), resulting in $NF_{\text{new}} \approx 4.95\text{ dB}$.
  • General Y-Factor Relation (Question 2a): Exact derivation for $T_c \neq T_0$ yields $F = \frac{ENR - Y (T_c/T_0 - 1)}{Y - 1}$.

docs.title: 3. Measurement Design and Simulation Summary
Y-Factor Simulation Results ($lab02_sim.grc$)
docs.text:
• At Receiver Gain = 40.0 dB ($ENR = 15\text{ dB}$): $N_{\text{off}} = -41.85\text{ dBFS}$, $N_{\text{on}} = -32.78\text{ dBFS} \implies Y = 9.07\text{ dB} \implies \mathbf{NF \approx 6.50\text{ dB}}$
  • At Receiver Gain = 10.0 dB ($ENR = 15\text{ dB}$): $N_{\text{off}} = -51.40\text{ dBFS}$, $N_{\text{on}} = -51.10\text{ dBFS} \implies Y = 0.30\text{ dB} \implies \mathbf{NF \approx 26.46\text{ dB}}$
  • Design Note: At low gain, $Y = 0.30\text{ dB} < 3\text{ dB}$ amplifies readout error sensitivity, justifying the requirement for an $ENR \approx 35\text{ dB}$ source per Table 4 design.

  • Two-Tone Intermodulation ($G = 0.0\text{ dB}, P_{\text{in}} = -30\text{ dBm}$): Fundamental output = $-10.00\text{ dBFS}$, IM3 products = $-25.79\text{ dBFS} \implies \Delta = +15.79\text{ dB} \implies \mathbf{IIP_3 \approx -22.1\text{ dBm}}$ (compared to theoretical $P_{1\text{dB}} + 9.6 = -13.7\text{ dBm}$).

docs.title: Laboratory Report 2: RF Noise Figure, $P_{1\text{dB}}$, and $\text{IIP}_3$ Parameters
docs.text: This report provides the analytical findings, completed experimental data tables, visual curve interpretations, and rigorous answers to all core and expansion questions formulated in Laboratory 2: RF Noise Figure and Linearity Parameters. Measurements were acquired using the dual ADALM-PLUTO Software-Defined Radio (SDR) testbench interfaced via the lab02_combined.grc GNU Radio flowgraph and the automated sweep GUI lab02_antenna_response_gui.py.

docs.title: 1. Device Noise Floor and Direct Method (Table 3 & Question 1)
docs.text:
In digital SDR architectures, internal power is represented in decibels relative to digital full-scale ($\text{dBFS}$). Converting digital power readings into absolute analog power in $\text{dBm}$ at the receiver input port requires the calibrated full-scale conversion factor $G_{FS}$:

$$P_{\text{in}}\,[\text{dBm}] = P_{\text{digital}}\,[\text{dBFS}] - G_{FS}$$

For the ADALM-PLUTO receiver under the baseline calibrated manual gain setting of $\text{rf_gain} = 40.2\text{ dB}$, the nominal conversion factor is established as $G_{FS} = 20.0\text{ dB}$, establishing that $0\text{ dBFS}$ corresponds to $-20.0\text{ dBm}$ of analog input power.

With the receiver input SMA port left open (unconnected termination), baseline digital noise power $N_{\text{off}}$ was acquired across three gain settings using the wideband noise channel filter ($B_n \approx 400\text{ kHz}$). The direct noise figure is estimated via:

$$\text{NF}{\text{direct}}\,[\text{dB}] \approx N{\text{off}}\,[\text{dBFS}] - G_{FS} - 10\log_{10}\left(\frac{B_n}{1\text{ Hz}}\right) - (-174\text{ dBm/Hz}) \approx N_{\text{off}}\,[\text{dBFS}] + 97.98\text{ dB}$$

At lower front-end gains ($29.7\text{ dB}$ and $40.2\text{ dB}$), the measured digital noise power hovers at $\approx -74\text{ dBFS}$, which is set by internal Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) quantization noise and digital baseband noise. At the maximum gain of $49.6\text{ dB}$, the amplified analog front-end thermal noise overcomes the ADC quantization floor, causing the digital reading to rise to $-66.20\text{ dBFS}$. Because the direct estimation formula presumes a static conversion factor $G_{FS} = 20\text{ dB}$ regardless of gain, it produces an erroneous apparent NF increase at $49.6\text{ dB}$, demonstrating why the direct method fails under varying front-end gain conditions.

docs.title: Question 1: Direct Method vs. $Y$-Factor Method Requirements
docs.text:
Prompt: What quantities does the direct method require that the $Y$-Factor method does not?

Answer: The direct method depends strictly on knowing three absolute system parameters: 1. Absolute Conversion Factor / Gain ($G_{FS}$): The precise hardware gain and full-scale calibration linking $\text{dBFS}$ to $\text{dBm}$. Any systematic calibration inaccuracy in $G_{FS}$ creates an identical, decibel-for-decibel error in the extracted noise figure. 2. Equivalent Noise Bandwidth ($B_n$): The exact integrated brick-wall noise bandwidth of the digital FIR channel filter. 3. Absolute Thermal Noise Power Reference: Explicit calibration against the theoretical input thermal noise density $k T_0 = -174\text{ dBm/Hz}$ at reference temperature $T_0 = 290\text{ K}$.

In contrast, the $Y$-Factor method relies exclusively on a relative power ratio $Y = N_{\text{on}} / N_{\text{off}}$ and the known Excess Noise Ratio ($\text{ENR}$) of the noise source. Because internal receiver gain, filter bandwidth, and digital scale factors affect $N_{\text{on}}$ and $N_{\text{off}}$ identically, they cancel completely out of the ratio $Y$, rendering the $Y$-Factor method fully independent of receiver gain, filter bandwidth, and digital scale calibrations.

docs.title: 2. Noise Figure via the $Y$-Factor Method (Table 4 & Question 2)
docs.text:
Broadband Gaussian noise generated by the transmitting PLUTO SDR was injected into the receiver port through a fixed 30-dB external safety pad ($A_{\text{pad}} = 30\text{ dB}$). Under nominal transmitter attenuation ($A_{tx} = 58.5\text{ dB}$), the effective excess noise ratio referenced to the receiver input is:

$$\text{ENR}{\text{eff}} = 73.4 - A{tx} = 73.4 - 58.5 \approx 15.0\text{ dB}$$

The $Y$-factor and receiver noise figure are computed via:

$$Y\,[\text{dB}] = N_{\text{on}}\,[\text{dBFS}] - N_{\text{off}}\,[\text{dBFS}]$$

$$\text{NF}\,[\text{dB}] = \text{ENR}{\text{eff}}\,[\text{dB}] - 10\log{10}\left(10^{Y\,[\text{dB}]/10} - 1\right)$$

When front-end RF gain is low, the noise contribution of the mixer, baseband PGAs, and downstream ADC quantization noise dominates the receiver cascade.

docs.title: Question 2: Limits on $Y$-Factor and Error Sensitivity Analysis
docs.text:
Prompt: Why should $Y$ be neither too small nor too large? For the smallest $Y$ in your table, calculate the effect of a 0.1 dB reading error on the calculated noise figure.

Answer: Why $Y$ cannot be too small ($Y < 3\text{ dB}$): As $Y \to 0\text{ dB}$ ($Y_{\text{linear}} \to 1$), the denominator $(10^{Y/10}-1) \to 0$. In this regime, the derivative $|d\text{NF}/dY|$ diverges toward infinity, meaning minute measurement noise or instrument flicker produces extreme errors in computed noise figure. * Why $Y$ cannot be too large ($Y > 15\text{ dB}$):* An excessively large $Y$ requires high injected noise power that drives receiver mixers, baseband filters, and ADCs into non-linear compression during the ON state, violating the prerequisite of linear operation.

Mathematical Error Sensitivity Derivation: Differentiating $\text{NF} = \text{ENR} - 10\log_{10}(10^{Y/10}-1)$ with respect to $Y$ (in decibels):

$$\frac{d\text{NF}}{dY} = -\frac{10^{Y/10}}{10^{Y/10}-1} = -\frac{1}{1 - 10^{-Y/10}}$$

Taking the smallest measured $Y$-factor in Table 4 ($Y = 0.80\text{ dB}$ at $834\text{ MHz}$, $\text{rf_gain} = 29.7\text{ dB}$):

$$10^{-0.80/10} = 10^{-0.08} \approx 0.8318$$

$$\left|\frac{d\text{NF}}{dY}\right| = \frac{1}{1 - 0.8318} = \frac{1}{0.1682} \approx 5.94\text{ dB/dB}$$

Therefore, an instrument reading error of merely $\delta Y = \pm 0.10\text{ dB}$ induces a large noise figure error of:

$$\delta\text{NF} \approx 5.94 \times 0.10\text{ dB} \approx \pm\mathbf{0.59\text{ dB}}$$

By contrast, for $Y = 6.60\text{ dB}$ ($\text{rf_gain} = 40.2\text{ dB}$), the sensitivity factor is only $|d\text{NF}/dY| \approx 1.28$, meaning a $0.1\text{ dB}$ error shifts NF by just $\pm 0.13\text{ dB}$.

docs.title: Question 3: Output Level at Compression and Primary Limiting Mechanism
docs.text:
Prompt: At the compression point, what was the output level in dBFS? What do you conclude regarding the limiting factor (ADC vs. analog stages)?

Answer: At the 1-dB compression point, the measured fundamental output level was $-8.0\text{ dBFS}$. For higher input drives, the output power saturates abruptly into a hard plateau at $-6.50\text{ dBFS}$.

  • In purely analog RF stages (e.g., LNA or passive mixer saturation), gain compression rolls off smoothly and progressively over a wide dynamic range ($> 15\text{ dB}$).
  • In this receiver, the transfer curve exhibits sharp, abrupt saturation within a few decibels of digital full scale ($0\text{ dBFS}$).

Conclusion: The dominant physical limiting factor is digital ADC full-scale clipping and baseband programmable gain amplifier (PGA) saturation, rather than analog front-end LNA compression.

docs.title: 4. Two-Tone Intermodulation Test and $\text{IIP}_3$ (Table 6 & Questions 4, 5)

Two equal-amplitude tones were injected at $f_1 = f_c + 300\text{ kHz}$ and $f_2 = f_c + 400\text{ kHz}$ ($\Delta f = 100\text{ kHz}$) at $\text{rf_gain} = 40.2\text{ dB}$. Input tone power was swept from $-70.0\text{ dBFS}$ to $-54.0\text{ dBFS}$. The intermodulation distance is $\Delta = P_{\text{fund}} - P_{\text{IMD3}}$, and the input third-order intercept point is computed as:

$$\text{IIP}3 = P{\text{in}} + \frac{\Delta}{2}$$

  • Mean Calculated $\text{IIP}_3$: $\mathbf{-53.8\text{ dBFS} \quad (-73.8\text{ dBm})}$.
  • Intercept-to-Compression Distance: $\text{IIP}3 - P{1\text{dB}} = -53.8 - (-66.5) = \mathbf{+12.7\text{ dB}}$.

docs.title: Question 4: Measured $\text{IMD}_3$ Slope and Validity of $\text{IIP}_3$
docs.text:
Prompt: What was the measured slope of the third-order intermodulation products? If it differs from 3, what conclusion do you draw regarding the nonlinear mechanism, and what is the validity of your $\text{IIP}_3$ value?

Answer: The measured $\text{IMD}_3$ product slope is $1.10\text{ dB/dB}$, which departs markedly from the theoretical weakly nonlinear slope of $3.0\text{ dB/dB}$.

  1. Nonlinear Mechanism: This slope anomaly demonstrates that intermodulation is not generated solely by receiver internal small-signal third-order Taylor polynomial distortion. As documented in the troubleshooting guide (Table 9 of the manual), when the transmitting PLUTO SDR operates near full output scale, its transmitted output already contains source-generated intermodulation products that scale $\approx 1:1$ with transmit power. Furthermore, digital ADC clipping introduces piecewise-linear threshold distortion that does not follow power-series mathematics.
  2. Validity of $\text{IIP}_3$: Because the fundamental premise of a $3:1$ intercept slope is violated, the calculated value of $\text{IIP}_3 = -53.8\text{ dBFS}$ cannot be interpreted as an ideal asymptotic small-signal third-order intercept point. Rather, it represents an apparent or empirical intercept metric valid only within the specific testing window.

docs.title: Question 5: Comparison of $\text{IIP}3 - P{1\text{dB}}$ with 9.6 dB and Peak Envelope Dynamics
docs.text:
Prompt: Compare $\text{IIP}3 - P{1\text{dB}}$ with 9.6 dB. Why does compression begin earlier in two-tone tests than in single-tone tests?

Answer: Numerical Comparison: The measured difference is $\text{IIP}3 - P{1\text{dB}} = -53.8 - (-66.5) = \mathbf{+12.7\text{ dB}}$, which is moderately higher than the canonical $9.6\text{ dB}$ offset predicted for an ideal memoryless third-order polynomial nonlinearity, due to non-ideal slope compression and ADC clipping dynamics. * Why Two-Tone Compression Occurs Earlier:* In a single-tone excitation of voltage amplitude $V_0$, peak instantaneous voltage is $V_{\text{peak}} = V_0$, giving peak envelope power $\text{PEP} = V_0^2 / (2R) = P_{\text{avg}}$. In a two-tone test where each tone has amplitude $V_0$, constructive interference occurs whenever the carriers align in phase:

$$V_{\text{peak, 2-tone}} = V_0 + V_0 = 2 V_0$$

Because instantaneous electrical power scales quadratically with voltage ($V^2$), peak envelope power is:

$$\text{PEP} \propto (2 V_0)^2 = 4 V_0^2 \implies \mathbf{+6.0\text{ dB higher than a single tone of equal amplitude}}$$

Consequently, the composite envelope reaches the receiver ADC full-scale saturation limit 6 dB earlier in per-tone input power than a single-tone stimulus.

Primary Operational Passband ($1.65\text{ GHz} - 1.76\text{ GHz}$): A dominant, smooth global resonance peak reaches $-28.80\text{ dB}$ at $1.70\text{ GHz}$. The extracted 3-dB bandwidth of $110.0\text{ MHz}$ yields a fractional bandwidth of $\text{FBW} = (110 / 1700) \times 100\% \approx 6.5\%$, typical of a tuned half-wave dipole or matched blade monopole antenna. 2. Secondary Multi-Band Resonant Peaks: * Sub-1 GHz Cellular Peak ($\approx 1.02\text{ GHz}$): A distinct local peak reaches $\approx -31.8\text{ dB}$ near $1.0\text{ GHz}$, matching the commercial GSM-900 / LTE cellular mobile uplink band. * 2.4 GHz ISM Band Peak ($\approx 2.44\text{ GHz}$): A pronounced resonance peak reaches $\approx -33.5\text{ dB}$ directly across the $2.40 - 2.48\text{ GHz}$ Industrial, Scientific, and Medical (ISM) band (Wi-Fi and Bluetooth). Electrically Small Mismatch Fluctuations ($< 900\text{ MHz}$): Below $900\text{ MHz}$, the curve exhibits severe rapid fluctuations and deep nulls plunging down to $-73\text{ dB}$ at $\approx 550\text{ MHz}$. At these low frequencies, the wavelength is long ($\lambda \approx 50 - 75\text{ cm}$), making the physical antenna electrically small ($l \ll \lambda/2$). The resulting large capacitive reactance creates severe impedance mismatch ($\Gamma \approx 1$) and negligible radiation efficiency. 4. High-Frequency Path Loss Rolloff ($> 2.5\text{ GHz}$): Beyond the 2.44 GHz ISM peak, received power drops monotonically down to $-63\text{ dB}$ at $3.0\text{ GHz}$. This steady attenuation follows the Friis transmission law, where free-space path loss increases with $f^2$, compounded by increased dielectric losses in SMA coaxial cables.

docs.title: Question 7: Maximum Dynamic Range and Blocker Tolerance
docs.text:
Prompt: At which gain is dynamic range ($P_{1\text{dB}} - N_{\text{floor}}$) maximized? Which gain setting should be chosen to receive a weak signal in the presence of a strong adjacent blocker, and why?

Answer: 1. Maximum Dynamic Range: Both linear dynamic range ($P_{1\text{dB}} - N_{\text{floor}} = 38.0\text{ dB}$) and Spurious-Free Dynamic Range ($\text{SFDR} = 33.8\text{ dB}$) reach their global peak at the nominal gain setting of $40.2\text{ dB}$. 2. Weak Signal Reception with Strong Adjacent Blocker: One must select the nominal or lower gain setting ($40.2\text{ dB}$ or lower), and never the maximum gain ($49.6\text{ dB}$). At maximum gain, input $P_{1\text{dB}}$ collapses to $-76.0\text{ dBFS}$ ($-96.0\text{ dBm}$). A strong adjacent blocker would immediately overdrive the receiver into hard ADC clipping, generating reciprocal mixing and cross-modulation distortion that completely blinds the receiver to the weak desired signal. Nominal gain preserves $10\text{ dB}$ more linearity headroom while maintaining near-optimum noise figure.

Mandatory Analysis 1: NF and Linearity vs. Gain (SFDR Argument)
docs.text: Plotting NF and $\text{IIP}_3$ against receiver gain exhibits two opposing trends. Below $40\text{ dB}$ gain, NF improves sharply ($\approx -1.13\text{ dB/dB}$), while linearity degrades at $-1.0\text{ dB/dB}$. Above $40\text{ dB}$ gain, NF reaches diminishing returns ($\approx -0.05\text{ dB/dB}$), but linearity continues to degrade at $-1.0\text{ dB/dB}$. The optimal trade-off that maximizes intermodulation-free dynamic range lies at $\text{rf_gain} \approx 40.2\text{ dB}$, where $\text{SFDR} = 33.8\text{ dB}$ is maximized.

docs.title: Question 8 (Expansion Question): Why Increasing Receiver Gain Does Not Continuously Improve Sensitivity
docs.text:
Prompt: Why does increasing receiver gain not continuously improve sensitivity? Quantify your answer using your experimental data.

Answer: Receiver sensitivity represents the minimum detectable input signal power $S_{\text{min}}$ required to achieve a specified signal-to-noise ratio $\text{SNR}_{\text{min}}$:

$$S_{\text{min}}\,[\text{dBm}] = -174\text{ dBm/Hz} + \text{NF}\,[\text{dB}] + 10\log_{10}(B) + \text{SNR}_{\text{min}}\,[\text{dB}]$$

Sensitivity depends directly on the Noise Figure ($\text{NF}$), not on gain. Gain amplifies both incoming signal and input thermal noise equally, preserving SNR. According to Friis' cascaded noise formula:

$$F_{\text{total}} = F_{\text{LNA}} + \frac{F_{\text{mixer}}-1}{G_{\text{LNA}}} + \frac{F_{\text{ADC}}-1}{G_{\text{LNA}} G_{\text{mixer}}}$$

As front-end gain $G_{\text{LNA}}$ is increased, downstream noise contributions are suppressed until total noise factor converges asymptotically to the intrinsic noise figure of the first LNA stage ($F_{\text{total}} \to F_{\text{LNA}}$).

  • Quantitative Evidence from Our Measurements:
  • Increasing gain from $29.7\text{ dB}$ to $40.2\text{ dB}$ ($+10.5\text{ dB}$ gain) reduces NF by $11.91\text{ dB}$ (from $21.38\text{ dB}$ down to $9.47\text{ dB}$), improving sensitivity by nearly $12\text{ dB}$.
  • Increasing gain further from $40.2\text{ dB}$ to $49.6\text{ dB}$ ($+9.4\text{ dB}$ gain) yields a negligible NF reduction of merely $0.50\text{ dB}$ (from $9.47\text{ dB}$ down to $8.97\text{ dB}$).
  • Severe Linearity Penalty: While sensitivity improves by only $0.5\text{ dB}$, input $P_{1\text{dB}}$ degrades by $9.5\text{ dB}$ (from $-86.5\text{ dBm}$ down to $-96.0\text{ dBm}$), and SFDR deteriorates by $6.0\text{ dB}$. Beyond the point where LNA noise dominates, additional gain provides zero practical sensitivity benefit while degrading dynamic range and blocker resilience.

1. Why FM is More Immune to Noise than AM
docs.text:
In Amplitude Modulation (AM), information is encoded directly into the instantaneous amplitude of the high-frequency carrier. Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN) from the channel adds algebraically to this envelope, making it mathematically impossible to eliminate noise without altering the original message.

Conversely, in Frequency Modulation (FM), the envelope amplitude remains strictly constant ($A$), and the message is encoded entirely within the instantaneous phase and frequency: $$s(t) = A \cos\big(2\pi f_c t + \varphi(t)\big)$$ This structural property provides two fundamental noise-rejection mechanisms: 1. Amplitude Hard-Limiting: A receiver limiter (or in discrete SDR, taking the angular phase $\arg(\cdot)$) strips away all spurious amplitude variations caused by channel fading, atmospheric interference, and thermal noise without distorting the underlying message. 2. Bandwidth-for-SNR Trade-Off: Above threshold, the post-detection output signal-to-noise ratio ($\text{SNR}_o$) scales quadratically with the frequency deviation ratio $(\Delta f / W)^2$: $$\text{SNR}_o \propto \left(\frac{\Delta f}{W}\right)^2 \text{CNR}$$ Increasing the frequency deviation widens the occupied spectrum, which in turn drastically suppresses detected baseband noise.

docs.title: 2. The Cost of the FM Advantage
docs.text: The superior noise rejection of FM is traded directly against substantial radio spectrum consumption. According to Carson's bandwidth rule: $$B_T \approx 2(\Delta f + f_{\max})$$ While a standard AM voice transmission occupies only $2W \approx 10\text{ kHz}$, commercial Wideband FM (WFM) allocates roughly $200\text{ kHz}$ per broadcast channel—an approximately twentyfold increase in spectrum usage.

docs.title: 3. The Threshold Effect and Catastrophic Breakdown
docs.text: The quadratic noise suppression in FM holds only when the input Carrier-to-Noise Ratio ($\text{CNR}$) exceeds a critical threshold ($\text{CNR}_{\text{th}} \approx 10\text{ dB}$). When $\text{CNR}$ falls below this boundary: * The noise phasor occasionally exceeds the carrier phasor in magnitude, sweeping the resultant vector around the origin and inducing a full $2\pi$ phase wrap-around (phase slip). * Because the discriminator differentiates phase to extract audio, this rapid $2\pi$ step manifests as a sharp Dirac-like impulse in time, heard as an audible "click" or "pop". * As the signal weakens further, the arrival rate of clicks accelerates exponentially, destroying phase coherence and driving the output $\text{SNR}_o$ into a steep, catastrophic cliff. Unlike AM, where audio degrades gradually into background static, an FM signal drops off abruptly from near-flawless fidelity into complete unintelligibility.

docs.title: Task 2: Theoretical Problems & Analytical Solutions
1. Single-Tone Bessel Expansion and Carson's Bandwidth
docs.text:
For a single-tone message $m(t) = \cos(2\pi f_m t)$, the instantaneous phase is: $$\varphi(t) = 2\pi\Delta f \int_0^t \cos(2\pi f_m \tau) d\tau = \frac{\Delta f}{f_m} \sin(2\pi f_m t) = \beta \sin(2\pi f_m t)$$ where $\beta = \frac{\Delta f}{f_m}$ is the modulation index.

The real bandpass signal is expressed as: $$s(t) = \text{Re}\left{ A e^{j(2\pi f_c t + \beta \sin(2\pi f_m t))} \right} = A \cdot \text{Re}\left{ e^{j 2\pi f_c t} \cdot e^{j \beta \sin(2\pi f_m t)} \right}$$ Applying the Jacobi-Anger expansion identity: $$e^{j \beta \sin(\theta)} = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{+\infty} J_n(\beta) e^{j n \theta}$$ Substituting $\theta = 2\pi f_m t$ and extracting the real part yields Equation (2): $$s(t) = A \sum_{n=-\infty}^{+\infty} J_n(\beta) \cos\big(2\pi(f_c + n f_m)t\big)$$

  • Carson's Bandwidth Calculation ($B_T \approx 2(\Delta f + f_{\max})$):
  • Mono broadcast ($f_{\max} = 15\text{ kHz}$, $\Delta f = 75\text{ kHz}$): $$B_{T,\text{mono}} = 2(75 + 15) = 180\text{ kHz}$$
  • Stereo multiplex ($f_{\max} = 53\text{ kHz}$, $\Delta f = 75\text{ kHz}$): $$B_{T,\text{stereo}} = 2(75 + 53) = 256\text{ kHz}$$
  • Comparison with Broadcast Channel Spacing: Commercial FM channels are spaced by $200\text{ kHz}$. The $180\text{ kHz}$ mono transmission fits comfortably within the $200\text{ kHz}$ channel allocation and is closest to this standard grid.

docs.title: 2. Carrier Nulls and Deviation Calibration
docs.text:
The amplitude of the center carrier line ($f_c$) is governed by the zero-order Bessel function $J_0(\beta)$. The carrier completely disappears when $J_0(\beta) = 0$. The first two positive roots of $J_0(\beta)$ are: $$\beta_1 \approx 2.4048 \approx 2.405, \quad \beta_2 \approx 5.5201 \approx 5.520$$ For a test tone of $f_m = 1\text{ kHz}$, the corresponding frequency deviations are: $$\Delta f_1 = \beta_1 f_m = 2.405 \times 1\text{ kHz} = 2405\text{ Hz}$$ $$\Delta f_2 = \beta_2 f_m = 5.520 \times 1\text{ kHz} = 5520\text{ Hz}$$

  • Calibration Procedure: A pure $1\text{ kHz}$ sinusoidal audio tone is fed into the FM transmitter while monitoring the RF output on a spectrum analyzer (or an SDR FFT sink). Starting from zero, the input audio amplitude is slowly increased. The center carrier peak at $f_c$ decreases until it drops into a sharp null and vanishes. At this exact point, $\beta = 2.405$, confirming that the transmitter's frequency deviation is calibrated precisely to $\Delta f = 2405\text{ Hz}$ without requiring a specialized deviation meter.

docs.title: 3. Discrete Phase Discriminator Linearity and Limits
docs.text: The numerical discriminator computes the angular difference between two successive complex samples: $$y[n] = \arg(x[n] x^[n-1]) = \arg\left(e^{j(\varphi[n] - \varphi[n-1])}\right)$$ Because the principal branch of the argument function $\arg(\cdot)$ is constrained to $(-\pi, +\pi]$, the phase difference between consecutive samples must not wrap around: $$|\varphi[n] - \varphi[n-1]| = |k_f m[n]| < \pi$$ Since $|m[n]| \le 1$, this condition reduces to: $$k_f = \frac{2\pi\Delta f}{f_s} < \pi \implies \Delta f < \frac{f_s}{2}$$ * Maximum Detectable Deviation at $f_s = 240\text{ kHz}$: $$\Delta f_{\max} = \frac{240\text{ kHz}}{2} = 120\text{ kHz}$$ * Effect of Entering $2\Delta f$ in Receiver Gain:* The discriminator gain is defined as $\text{Gain} = \frac{f_s}{2\pi \Delta f_{\text{rx}}}$. If the receiver mistakenly assumes $\Delta f_{\text{rx}} = 2\Delta f_{\text{actual}}$, the gain is halved: $$\hat{m}[n] = \frac{f_s}{2\pi (2\Delta f)} \cdot \left(\frac{2\pi\Delta f}{f_s} m[n]\right) = \frac{1}{2} m[n]$$ The output audio amplitude is attenuated by exactly $50\%$ (a $6.02\text{ dB}$ loss in volume), while remaining completely linear and free of distortion.

docs.title: 4. Comparison: Discriminator vs. PLL Frequency Detector
docs.text:
Comparison Metric Non-Coherent Discriminator (Quadrature Demod) Coherent PLL (PLL Frequency Detector) Design Parameters Only linear scaling gain: $\text{Gain} = \frac{f_s}{2\pi\Delta f}$ Loop Bandwidth, damping factor, Min/Max Phase Performance Above Threshold Completely linear; parabolic output noise PSD ($f^2$) Identical to discriminator; linear frequency tracking Performance Near Threshold Exhibits sudden click impulses around $\text{CNR} \approx 10\text{ dB}$ Threshold Extension: Delays threshold by $2\text{ to }3\text{ dB}$ Carrier Offset Sensitivity Highly robust; carrier offset $\delta f$ produces a harmless constant DC offset Vulnerable; if $\delta f$ exceeds lock range, the loop loses lock entirely Computational Complexity Extremely low (one complex multiply + one $\arg(\cdot)$) Moderate to high (phase error, loop filter, NCO updates)
  • Why the PLL Threshold Advantage Increases with Large $\beta$: When $\beta \gg 1$, the Carson bandwidth $B_T \approx 2\Delta f$ is vastly wider than the baseband information bandwidth $W$. A non-coherent discriminator must accept all thermal noise across the entire transmission bandwidth $B_T$. In contrast, the PLL acts as a dynamic tracking filter whose effective noise bandwidth $B_L$ is matched only to the message rate ($B_L \ll B_T$). By rejecting out-of-band noise prior to nonlinear phase detection, the PLL suppresses phase slips, significantly improving threshold performance for wideband signals.

docs.title: 5. FM Improvement Trade-off Under Constant Received Power
docs.text:
Substituting $\text{CNR} = \frac{P_c}{N_0 B_T}$ into Equation (8): $$\text{SNR}o = \frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{\Delta f}{W}\right)^2 \frac{B_T}{W} \left(\frac{P_c}{N_0 B_T}\right) = \frac{3}{2}\frac{(\Delta f)^2}{W^3}\frac{P_c}{N_0}$$ Assuming constant received carrier power $P_c$ and noise density $N_0$, doubling the frequency deviation ($\Delta f \to 2\Delta f$) yields: $$\text{SNR}{o,\text{new}} = 4 \times \text{SNR}{o,\text{old}} \implies 10\log{10}(4) \approx 6.02\text{ dB improvement}$$

  • Threshold Power Shift: The threshold boundary occurs at a constant carrier-to-noise ratio: $$\text{CNR}{\text{th}} = \frac{P{c,\text{th}}}{N_0 B_T} = 10\text{ dB} = 10 \implies P_{c,\text{th}} = 10 N_0 B_T$$ Because $B_T \approx 2(\Delta f + W)$, doubling $\Delta f$ approximately doubles the occupied channel bandwidth $B_T$ (for wideband FM). Consequently: $$\frac{P_{c,\text{th},\text{new}}}{P_{c,\text{th},\text{old}}} \approx \frac{B_{T,\text{new}}}{B_{T,\text{old}}} \approx 2 \implies 10\log_{10}(2) \approx 3.01\text{ dB}$$ To remain above the noise threshold, the transmitter must supply approximately $3\text{ dB}$ more RF power.

docs.title: 6. Carrier Frequency Offset Analysis
docs.text:
If the received carrier possesses an unknown frequency offset $\delta f$, the instantaneous frequency becomes: $$f_i(t) = f_c + \delta f + \Delta f m(t)$$ The discrete sample phase difference across interval $T_s = 1/f_s$ is: $$\Delta \varphi[n] = 2\pi (f_i - f_c) T_s = \frac{2\pi}{f_s}\big(\delta f + \Delta f m[n]\big)$$ Applying the discriminator gain $\text{Gain} = \frac{f_s}{2\pi\Delta f}$: $$\hat{m}[n] = \frac{f_s}{2\pi\Delta f} \cdot \frac{2\pi}{f_s}\big(\delta f + \Delta f m[n]\big) = m[n] + \frac{\delta f}{\Delta f}$$ The carrier offset appears as a pure, frequency-independent DC bias equal to $\frac{\delta f}{\Delta f}$.

  • Numerical Offset Calculation at $434\text{ MHz}$ ($30\text{ ppm}$ tolerance): $$\delta f = 434\text{ MHz} \times 30 \times 10^{-6} = 13.02\text{ kHz}$$
  • Impact on a Narrowband Channel ($B_T = 16\text{ kHz}$): A narrowband channel filter centered at baseband has a one-sided passband edge of only: $$\frac{B_T}{2} = \frac{16\text{ kHz}}{2} = 8\text{ kHz}$$ Because the carrier offset $\delta f = 13.02\text{ kHz}$ exceeds the $8\text{ kHz}$ cutoff, the entire FM spectrum is shifted out of the filter's passband. This causes severe signal attenuation, extreme harmonic distortion, and complete loss of reception.

docs.title: Task 5: Risk Analysis and Failure Mitigation
1. Hardware Damage via Direct RF Overdrive (Critical Safety Risk)
docs.text:
• Failure Mechanism: Connecting the PlutoSDR TX port directly to the RX port without the mandatory $30\text{ dB}$ hardware attenuator, or setting the software internal attenuation to $0\text{ dB}$.
  • Consequence: Power delivered to the receiver exceeds the maximum absolute damage rating ($-10\text{ dBm}$), permanently destroying the receiver's Low-Noise Amplifier (LNA).
  • Mitigation Protocol: Both team members must physically verify that the inline $30\text{ dB}$ coaxial attenuator is connected to the RX port before executing the flowgraph. Furthermore, the Attenuation TX1 (dB) parameter in the PlutoSDR Sink must be verified to be set to $\ge 35\text{ dB}$.

docs.title: 2. Audio Distortion via Overly Constrained PLL Bandwidth
docs.text:
• Failure Mechanism: Setting the Loop Bandwidth parameter of the PLL Frequency Detector to an excessively small value (e.g., $<0.05$) in an attempt to suppress noise.
  • Consequence: The loop phase response becomes too slow to track rapid frequency deviations caused by high audio dynamics. The PLL slips cycles, drops phase lock, and produces severe non-linear audio clipping and clicking.
  • Mitigation Protocol: Initialize the loop with a conservative bandwidth ($LB \approx 0.35$). Progressively reduce the bandwidth in small increments while observing the FFT sink and listening for the onset of audio distortion.

docs.title: 3. De-emphasis Standard Mismatch
docs.text:
• Failure Mechanism: Leaving the FM Deemphasis block at its default GNU Radio parameter value of $\tau = 75\ \mu\text{s}$ (the North American / South Korean standard).
  • Consequence: Local Iranian and European FM broadcasts are transmitted with a $\tau = 50\ \mu\text{s}$ pre-emphasis curve. Applying a $75\ \mu\text{s}$ low-pass filter at the receiver excessively attenuates higher audio frequencies, producing muffled, lifeless sound.
  • Mitigation Protocol: Explicitly configure the Tau parameter of the FM Deemphasis block to 50e-6 ($50\ \mu\text{s}$) to match ITU-R BS.450 standards for region 1.
